name: The Doldrum Anchor

detectability.signature: metronomic pulse repeating at exactly 31-hour intervals with identical sensor returns each cycle

proximity: Persistent déjà vu as crews recognize events moments before they recur
Duplicate sensor contacts shadow every vessel's own transponder echo
contact: Vessels become caught in the loop, reliving the same 31-hour watch indefinitely
Actions taken in prior cycles persist as faint habits no one remembers forming
prolonged_exposure: Minds unravel under hundreds of identical repetitions, memory filing itself into circles
Ships are found drifting with crews who cannot say how many times they have spoken the same words

phenomena: Visible echoes of past events replaying identically on every cycle
Causality loops bleeding minor synchronicities into nearby systems
Debris and vessels frozen mid-trajectory, resuming their falls at each reset
opportunities: Hidden base location, since observers outside see only a repeating instant
Unique research opportunity to study causal recursion frame by frame
Ambush point against fleets that cannot remember previous attacks
known_incidents: The mining barge Grateful Ledger logged four hundred identical departures before a rescue tug noticed her weekly distress call never varied by a syllable
description: The Doldrum Anchor hangs in space like a becalmed sea given a border, a sphere two-tenths of an astronomical unit wide where nothing ever quite finishes happening. Its boundary shimmers with a slow silver pulse, and within it light itself seems to hesitate mid-crossing. Long-range sensors read the zone as a single heartbeat, repeated forever.

Every thirty-one hours the interior resets to its anchor state: the same debris positions, the same half-finished burns, the same ghosts of ionized exhaust. Ships entering between resets carry their changes forward until the wave passes through them, then find themselves back at the start with only instincts left over. Escape windows exist and can be charted; missing one costs another full cycle.

Salvage tugs found the Grateful Ledger after her four hundredth identical distress call, her crew cheerful and unable to explain why their coffee cups were all still full. The loop's regularity made it famous; its origin made it feared, for no natural process repeats so perfectly. Some surveyors insist the anchor state resembles the interior of an ancient beacon, but nothing has been proven.

Loop-crawlers now run guided excursions timed to the reset wave, advertising the safest dangerous place in the sector. Research stations hover permanently outside the pulse, harvesting recursion data thirty-one hours at a time. The old advice holds: enter on a fresh chime, count your cycles, and never trust a memory that feels like déjà vu.
